title: Exploring the use of quantum computing for facilitating spatially and temporally resolved models of a biological cell
authors: Muralikrishnan Gopalakrishnan Meena, Dileep Kishore, Jerry M. Parks, Luke Bertels, Dilipkumar N. Asthagiri, Travis Humble, Thomas L. Beck, Mitchel J. Doktycz
abstract: Whole-cell simulation, modeling all of a cell's functional systems over its life cycle, is an outstanding challenge in computational biology. Even the simplest living cell contains thousands of interacting proteins and metabolites (on the order of trillions of atoms) whose full functional dynamics spans roughly five orders of magnitude in space (nm to $μ$m) and nearly nineteen in time (fs to hours). Further, many of the governing physical and chemical properties remain incompletely characterized. Simulating such complex systems at fully atomistic resolution over a full cell cycle is computationally intractable on classical architectures, raising a central question: Can quantum computing offer a viable path to whole-cell simulations that integrate molecular- and systems-level complexity? This Perspective examines the potential of quantum computing across three hierarchical scales: atomistic-molecular modeling, metabolic and regulatory networks, and whole-cell spatial modeling. We present a complexity analysis comparing classical and quantum algorithms for representative biological problems, identifying regimes of substantial theoretical speedup under specified algorithmic assumptions. We highlight algorithmic developments designed to leverage both near-term exploratory and fault-tolerant quantum architectures, and discuss practical bottlenecks: data encoding overhead, system conditioning, measurement constraints, and hybrid quantum-HPC integration. Together, these results outline a roadmap for quantum-accelerated whole-cell modeling and the biological insights such multiscale frameworks may eventually enable.
summary: This paper explores using quantum computing to overcome the intractable computational barriers of whole-cell simulations. It analyzes how quantum algorithms can accelerate modeling across molecular dynamics, metabolic networks, and spatial reaction-diffusion processes. The work provides a roadmap detailing where quantum advantage is theoretically achievable for simulating life at its most complex scales.
main_problem: The central challenge is developing computationally tractable whole-cell simulations that integrate molecular, metabolic, and spatial dynamics across vast scales (nm to $\mu$m, fs to hours).
main_result: Quantum computing offers a potential path to accelerate these multi-scale biological simulations by providing theoretical speedups over classical methods for solving underlying linear systems and sampling rare events.
method: The paper systematically compares quantum algorithms (like VQE, QAOA, QLSA) against established classical techniques (MD, FBA, PDE solvers) across three hierarchical scales of biological modeling.
model_or_system: The system is a living cell containing trillions of interacting components. Modeling spans from atomistic electronic structure calculations to whole-cell reaction-diffusion master equations.
key_observables: Computational time required for simulating entire cell cycles (e.g., E. coli, Yeast), molecular energies, and free energy changes ($\Delta F$).
important_parameters: Spatial scales ($	ext{nm}$ to $\mu	ext{m}$), temporal scales ($	ext{fs}$ to hours), system size ($N$), and required accuracy ($\epsilon$, $\delta$).
main_assumptions: The feasibility relies on achieving fault-tolerant quantum architectures, and practical bottlenecks include data encoding overhead and hybrid integration strategies.
figures_summary: Figures compare computational time for whole-cell simulations (E. coli/Yeast) using classical vs. quantum solvers; tables detail algorithm comparisons across atomistic, network, and cell scales.
paper_structure: The paper is structured as a perspective examining the potential of quantum computing across three hierarchical modeling scales: atomistic-molecular, metabolic networks, and whole-cell spatial dynamics, providing complexity analyses for each.
why_interesting: It bridges fundamental quantum computation concepts (e.g., solving linear systems via QLSA) directly to complex, non-equilibrium biological processes, suggesting novel computational pathways for simulating open quantum/many-body systems in biology.
